document_metadata.title: 1、INT KITTREDGE'S APARTMENT LIVING ROOM DAWN
document_metadata.summary: Flan and Ouisa, shaken after a break-in, check for stolen items and recall their near-miss, fearing for their safety as they debate attending a wedding.

document_metadata.title: 35、INT COLLEGE DORM ROOM DAY
document_metadata.summary: Doug confronts his father, Dr. Fine, who claims there are two sides to the story and recounts returning home with a policeman, while a girl reacts in fear and others listen intently.

entities.name: Doug answers phone call from his father late at night
entities.description: Doug, awakened from sleep in his college dorm room, picks up a phone call from his father, Dr. Fine, initiating a tense and emotionally charged conversation.

entities.name: Dr. Fine confronts his son about personal accusations
entities.description: During a phone call, Dr. Fine responds defensively to what he perceives as accusations from his son, claiming he is being blamed for lacking interest in Doug's life and being a poor father.

entities.name: Doug expresses deep embarrassment and anger toward his father
entities.description: Doug reacts with outrage upon learning that his father gave house keys to a stranger who mentioned his name, calling him a cretin and expressing shame over their relationship.

entities.name: Doug reveals mother's allegations about Dr. Fine's past behavior
entities.description: Doug tells his father that his mother accused him of domestic violence, being a poor lover, and excessive drinking, using vivid and degrading metaphors to describe their marriage.

entities.name: Doug questions the purpose of his own existence
entities.description: Overwhelmed by the emotional weight of the conversation, Doug bitterly laments his father's actions and wonders why he was ever brought into the world.

entities.name: Two couples and Dr. Fine enter The Strand Bookstore
entities.description: Ouisa, Flan, Kitty, Larkin, and Dr. Fine arrive and walk into The Strand Bookstore, a large bookstore known for its extensive collection.

entities.description: Ouisa locates and takes down a copy of Sidney Poitier's autobiography titled 'This Life' from a bookshelf at The Strand.

entities.name: Ouisa reads a passage from Sidney Poitier's autobiography
entities.description: Ouisa reads aloud a passage from 'This Life' describing Poitier's awareness of his marriage deteriorating despite surface-level stability.

entities.name: Flan examines the photograph in the autobiography
entities.description: Flan takes the book from Ouisa and comments on a photo showing Sidney Poitier with his four daughters, noting the absence of sons.

entities.name: Scene shifts to the Morgan Library with Flan repeating the book title
entities.description: The narrative moves to the Morgan Library, where Flan restates that the book is called 'This Life,' recontextualizing the earlier event.

entities.description: A concert attendee echoes Flan's earlier observation by asking 'No sons?' in response to the mention of the photograph.

entities.name: Ouisa confirms the absence of sons in Sidney Poitier's family photo
entities.description: Ouisa responds to the concert-goer's question by emphatically confirming that there are no sons, only four daughters.

entities.name: Kitty expresses concern about the intruder's impact
entities.description: Back at The Strand, Kitty reacts to the situation by saying 'Oh dear,' reflecting unease about the young man who entered their lives.

entities.name: Ouisa reflects on the intruder's forceful entry into their lives
entities.description: Ouisa compares the young man's intrusion to a bulldozer, emphasizing how abruptly and disruptively he entered their personal world.

entities.name: Larkin comments on their group's professional achievements and openness
entities.description: Larkin observes that despite their societal roles—foundation director, art dealer, doctor—they allowed the stranger into their lives, questioning their own satisfaction and boundaries.

document_metadata.summary: Woody confronts his parents angrily for giving his cherished pink shirt, a gift for his transformed body, to a stranger, expressing deep betrayal and resentment.

entities.name: Ouisa presents yearbook and demands phone calls from students
entities.description: Ouisa hands over a copy of a yearbook and instructs a group of students to obtain phone numbers of their classmates from the same boarding school, initiating a coordinated effort to contact their peers.

entities.description: Dr. Fine confronts the students' hesitation, pointing out their usual frequent phone use and criticizing their sudden unwillingness to make nationwide calls.

entities.description: Tess frames the current situation as reminiscent of the McCarthy period, evoking themes of suspicion, political persecution, and mass surveillance.
